design_detail: In-depth narrative review by two kidney specialists (Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2008): pharmacology and metabolism (Figures 1 and 2), clinical syndromes (Table 1), acute kidney injury (Table 2), low blood sodium with a table of 32 reported cases (Table 3) and a figure of proposed mechanisms (Figure 3), and a treatment section that is not used here. No search method, dates or inclusion criteria are stated; 88 references, most of them case reports, letters and reviews, a few animal studies and one retrospective series.
can_establish: Which kinds of kidney injury and of low blood sodium had been described after ecstasy in case reports up to 2008, what the authors think are the likely mechanisms, and what they say about who was reported; and, from this card's reporting issues, where their statements go beyond the sources they cite.
cannot_establish: How often kidney injury or low sodium happens (for kidney injury the review itself says the incidence cannot be determined); which factor caused which case (case reports have no comparison); the size of any sex difference (the reports are selected); or anything independent of the primary papers, which the review reports second-hand and this reader has not read.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence base as described: case reports and letters (more than 25 reports of low sodium; single case reports for most kidney problems), a few case series, a human volunteer study of vasopressin, and animal studies; Table 3 lists 32 reported cases of low sodium from 21 sources (p. 1855).
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports show people who became ill and were written up; they say nothing about how many people took ecstasy and were not harmed. 10 of the 32 rows in Table 3 come from one California series and all 10 are deaths, 6 of them with no sodium recorded. The in-text citation range for the low-sodium case reports (references 48-68) includes a kidney-injury report (48), an analysis (59), a rat study (67) and a case series (68).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited report, as described: by history in case reports; in the one volunteer study cited, a dose given by the study team.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described in the review, not a study condition: three doses at a rave in the first kidney-injury case (1992); 'a single dose' in the vast majority of low-sodium cases (stated in the text; Table 3 has no dose column, p. 1855); five tablets in the one case described in detail (pp. 1855-1856). In the volunteer vasopressin study cited, a small single dose was given to eight men (p. 1856).
exposure.polysubstance: Table 3 has no column for other substances. The review says attributing vasculitis to ecstasy is difficult because other substances are often taken (p. 1854).

comparison.controls: None in the review. Case reports have no comparison; the one controlled human experiment described compared vasopressin before and after a dose in eight men.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body size, kidney function, fluid intake, exertion, heat, other drugs and genetic differences in metabolism are mentioned as possible factors but not measured in the reports the review describes.

outcomes.instruments: As reported in the cited papers: serum and urine sodium and osmolality, plasma vasopressin, creatine kinase, creatinine; scans. The review states that no case of kidney injury after ecstasy had a kidney biopsy (p. 1854).
outcomes.validity_norms: Low sodium is described as 'usually' below 130 mEq/L (p. 1855); Table 3 includes two rows with a sodium of 130.
outcomes.operationalization: Case reports of kidney injury (Table 2) and of low sodium (Table 3), grouped by the reviewers' reading of the likely cause.

analysis.effect_sizes: As described, no pooled analysis. Death risk in people taking ecstasy for the first time estimated at 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 (Gore 1999, as cited, p. 1852). Kidney injury: incidence 'cannot be determined'; CK of 100,000 U/L or more in rhabdomyolysis cases (p. 1854); up to 31% of drug-related acute liver failure attributed to MDMA in one study (Andreu, as cited, p. 1854). Low sodium: more than 25 case reports; sodium 101-130 mEq/L; vast majority female, aged 15-30 (text, p. 1855). Table 3 (checked on a render of p. 1855): 32 rows, 27 F, 1 labelled W, 4 M; ages 14-30; 16 deaths, 15 recoveries, 1 not available; 10 rows (all deaths) from the California series, 6 of them with no sodium; Hartung's UK series (reference 68) is not in the table. The text says more than 85% of symptomatic cases were female (28 of 32 rows). The one detailed case: an 18-year-old woman after five tablets, sodium 136 then 130 mEq/L after 1,700 ml of water, plasma vasopressin 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6) (pp. 1855-1856). Vasopressin in eight volunteers rose from 1.14-1.88 to 2.46-9.16 pmol/L within 1 to 2 hours (Henry 1998, as cited, p. 1856).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection without a stated search. The review says some points against its own mechanism (sweat sodium loss 'likely marginal'; most reports lack significant hyperthermia; the incidence of kidney injury cannot be determined) but states other points more firmly in the abstract and conclusions than the text supports (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Case reports and a few series show that rhabdomyolysis with high temperature and exertion is the commonest described route to kidney injury, with single reports of other kinds; and that low blood sodium with brain swelling has been reported after ecstasy, mostly in young women who had drunk fluid, with vasopressin raised in a few cases and in eight volunteers. The review has no incidence figures for either.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the low sodium a 'perfect storm' of vasopressin release, polydipsia and ready fluids, and the Conclusions add drug-induced thirst and say young people who take a single dose are at risk. The text says a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized' (p. 1855), and no denominator is given for 'at risk'. The review says the California study found women had a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death, which that study did not show (it found no clear difference for death).

timeline.event: First case report of kidney injury after ecstasy: three doses at a rave, with seizures, rhabdomyolysis and clotting disorder (Fahal and colleagues, as described in this review).
First report of low sodium after ecstasy named in the review (Maxwell and colleagues, as described).
Vasopressin rises within 1 to 2 hours in eight healthy men given a small dose of MDMA (Henry and colleagues, as described).
UK poisons-service series of 17 people with low sodium after ecstasy (listed among the references, not tabulated).
A woman who drank 1,700 ml of water after five tablets and whose sodium fell from 136 to 130 mEq/L, with very high vasopressin (Brvar and colleagues, as described).
Loss of two transplanted kidneys from one donor with recent ecstasy use (Hurault de Ligny and colleagues, as described).
California poison-centre series of 545 reports, which the review summarises and mis-cites.

replication.where_it_stands: Kidney injury after ecstasy is known from case reports only; the commonest described route is muscle breakdown after exertion with overheating and too little fluid. Low blood sodium has been reported repeatedly, from single cases to a 545-report series, mostly in young women. Mechanisms (vasopressin release, fluid intake) are plausible and partly measured in volunteers, but no study read in this batch compares people who drank a lot with people who did not.

funding.affiliations_note: Two authors from the Division of Nephrology, University of Virginia.

what_would_settle_it: For kidney injury: a prospective registry of people attending emergency departments after MDMA, with creatinine and creatine kinase measured on arrival and at follow-up and a count of everyone who attended, so that an incidence could be estimated; kidney biopsy in unexplained cases. For low sodium: see the other cards in this batch (sodium measured on arrival, fluid intake recorded, comparison with people who drank similarly and stayed well).

domains.note: No search method, databases, dates or criteria; the Table 3 rows come from 21 sources and omit the largest UK series; the citation range for case reports includes papers that are not case reports.
No appraisal; case reports, letters, one retrospective series and animal studies are cited side by side as 'case reports' and 'controlled studies'.
The California series is cited as a 1998 case report; Table 1 is cited for sex data it does not contain; 'a single dose' is stated but not tabulated; six Table 3 rows have no sodium.
Mechanisms are mostly worded as 'likely' or 'hypothesized' in the text, but the abstract and Conclusions state drug-induced thirst as fact.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against
domains.note: Says the incidence of kidney injury cannot be determined and that sweat sodium loss is likely marginal, but concludes that young people taking a single dose are at risk with no denominator, and argues the female predominance is not a reporting bias without data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3). The overall judgment is not milder than its worst domain. Use it for the list of kinds of kidney injury and low sodium that had been described by 2008, for what the authors say is unknown, and for pointers to the primary reports; do not use it for how often either happens, for who is at risk, or for the California findings (read Rosenson 2007 instead).

key_findings.finding: The review says ecstasy toxicity is 'not attributable to overdose' in the usual sense: some people take it without harm, while others taking similar amounts have serious toxicity (Brown and Osterloh 1987, as cited). It gives an estimated death risk of 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 for people taking it for the first time (Gore 1999, as cited); the spread is 25-fold and no basis is shown.

Metabolism, as described from two other reviews: breakdown depends partly on the enzyme CYP2D6, which varies between people; slow metabolisers are said to be at higher risk because levels stay high; after repeated doses (even as few as two) metabolites can inhibit the enzyme, so there is 'the potential for increased toxicity with repeated dosing'. A metabolite, HMMA, is described as a more potent trigger of vasopressin release than MDMA itself, which the authors suggest could explain why low sodium is not seen in everyone.
key_findings.locator: Pharmacology, 3rd paragraph (p. 1852, continued on p. 1853, left column); p. 1853, right column, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Kidney injury: the review says most of the data come from case reports and that 'the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined'. The first case (1992) followed three doses at a rave, with seizures, rhabdomyolysis and a clotting disorder. The commonest described route is non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), mostly in people who had exerted themselves with inadequate fluid, impaired heat regulation and high temperature, made worse by a hot room; creatine kinase of 100,000 U/L or more is described; low volume and low blood pressure add to the injury.
key_findings.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, paragraphs 1-2 (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Other kidney problems are single case reports: transient proximal tubule dysfunction in an 18-year-old; necrotizing vasculitis in a 30-year-old man who had used ecstasy 10 days before and went on to kidney failure; loss of both transplanted kidneys from one donor with recent use; bladder-neck obstruction; and kidney injury after accelerated or malignant hypertension. The review says that no case of kidney injury after ecstasy had a kidney biopsy, and that attributing vasculitis to ecstasy is difficult because other substances are often taken. Liver failure after ecstasy is described, with a risk of kidney injury through hepatorenal syndrome; one study attributed up to 31% of drug-related acute liver failure to MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Acute Kidney Injury, right column (p. 1854); Table 2 (p. 1854); p. 1855, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Low sodium: more than 25 case reports since 1993; sodium on presentation 101 to 130 mEq/L; 'the vast majority' of cases were female, aged 15 to 30, and are said to have taken a single dose (not shown in Table 3). The cause is called dilutional and due to several interacting effects. Table 3 lists 32 cases (27 F, 1 W, 4 M; 16 deaths, 15 recoveries, 1 unknown), 10 of them from the California series (all deaths, 6 with no sodium recorded); the UK series of 17 is not tabulated.

Fluid and thirst: excessive water intake 'has been directly associated' with ecstasy, partly through 'chill out' areas offering free or cheap water; ecstasy-related dry mouth and thirst are described; whether ecstasy causes a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized'. The one detailed case: an 18-year-old woman, five tablets, severe headache and thirst, sodium 136 mEq/L, then 1,700 ml of water and a sodium of 130 mEq/L with plasma vasopressin of 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6) and urine osmolality 335 mOsm/kg. The authors say the availability of fluids and thirst are 'likely not enough' on their own, because the kidney can normally excrete water faster than it is drunk; kidney water excretion must also be impaired.
key_findings.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1855, right column); p. 1856, left column, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Vasopressin: said to rise within 1 to 2 hours of MDMA in controlled settings (eight healthy men given a small dose, from a baseline of 1.14-1.88 to 2.46-9.16 pmol/L, with a slight fall in sodium; other studies cited), and more with the metabolite HMMA; urine osmolality was inappropriately high in case reports (184-970 mOsm/kg). Sweat sodium loss is called 'likely marginal'; most low-sodium case reports lack significant hyperthermia; the authors conclude that increased water intake together with kidney water retention is the main driving force.
key_findings.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, left column, 2nd paragraph; right column, 3rd-4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sex: said to be highly associated with symptomatic low sodium; 'a review of published case reports' found more than 85% of symptomatic cases were female; the review says this was also documented in a 5-year California case review and that it 'does not reflect a bias' toward more women taking ecstasy because other complications are commoner in men (no data given). Suggested reasons are estrogen effects on the brain's sodium pump and vasopressin response, lower muscle mass and body weight (second-hand).

Conclusions: kidney injury is mostly pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis after rhabdomyolysis; low sodium is called a 'perfect storm' of drug-induced vasopressin release, drug-induced thirst and ready fluids; the authors say young people who take a single dose are at risk. The remaining sentences are advice and treatment and are not used.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says ecstasy leads to polydipsia (excess drinking) through its serotonin effects, and the Conclusions list drug-induced thirst as a main mechanism, but the text says whether ecstasy causes a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized', citing one case and a rat study.
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-induced thirst is a hypothesis in this review, not a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The California case review is cited as reference 49 (Ajaelo 1998, a case report) when it is reference 82 (Rosenson 2007). The review says it showed a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death in women; that study measured low sodium only in people who had a sodium test, found higher odds of coma in women with low sodium, and found no clear difference for death.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review overstates the California findings; read Rosenson 2007 for them.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 32 cases, but 6 rows (all deaths from the California series) have no sodium recorded, 16 of the 32 rows are deaths, one row has gender 'W', and the UK series of 17 (reference 68) is absent. The text says more than 25 case reports; the rows come from 21 sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table is not a count of cases and shows mostly the most severe reports; do not use it for the share of women or the share who died.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the vast majority of cases 'ingested a single dose', but Table 3 has no dose column, and the one detailed case took five tablets.
reporting_issues.consequence: The single-dose statement cannot be checked in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Female gender is described as 'highly associated' with symptoms, citing Table 1, which lists clinical syndromes and has no data on sex. The share of more than 85% is a count of published reports, and the argument that it is not a bias toward more women taking ecstasy has no data or reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex difference is from selected reports; it is not an estimate of risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The citation range for the low-sodium case reports (references 48-68) includes a kidney-injury report (48), an analysis (59), a rat study (67) and a case series (68). The 'controlled studies' of vasopressin rise within 1 to 2 hours (13, 69-72) include a study of isolated rat hypothalamus (71) and a study of people in a club (72).
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of case reports and the strength of the human vasopressin evidence are overstated.

reporting_issues.issue: No search method, databases, dates or inclusion criteria are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The set of cases is whatever the authors chose; absence of a kind of case does not mean it has not occurred.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1852-1860 (PDFs/MDMA/Campbell_2008_AgonyOfEcstasyKidney.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, Figure 3, Conclusions, disclosures and the reference list (read to check the citations noted above). Table 3 and the gender and Conclusions passages were checked on rendered images of printed pages 1855 and 1857.
